subtopic_detail: Psychiatric opinion on repeated shoplifting in an older adult with behavioural change
stem:
You are the consultation psychiatrist asked by a solicitor to assess a 64-year-old woman charged with shoplifting for the third time in 8 months. On each occasion she walked out of the same supermarket with items in her hand in full view of staff and made no attempt to conceal them or to leave quickly.

The items were sweets and magazines she did not need, and she has no financial hardship. She has no previous convictions of any kind over 64 years and no history of substance use.

She tells you flatly that she does not see what the fuss is about and shows no distress about the charges. She denies any build-up of tension before taking the items and denies any sense of relief afterwards.

Her husband reports that over 18 months she has begun eating large quantities of sweets, having previously disliked them, and that she now laughs when told bad news, including at his brother's funeral. She has stopped visiting her sister, whom she used to see weekly, and no longer asks about the grandchildren. Her mood is not low by her own account or his, her sleep and weight are stable and there is no psychotic symptom. Her Montreal Cognitive Assessment score is 28 out of 30 with marked difficulty on verbal fluency and on the trail making item.

data_table.Mental state: Flat and unconcerned about the charges, no tension-relief pattern described, no low mood, no psychotic symptoms
data_table.Cognition: Montreal Cognitive Assessment 28 out of 30 with marked impairment on verbal fluency and trail making
data_table.Collateral: New craving for sweet foods, laughter at distressing news, withdrawal from previously valued relationships over 18 months, no previous convictions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Advise the solicitor that no psychiatric diagnosis is present and she is fit to plead
options.rationale: Closing the assessment at this point misses a syndrome that is plainly emerging in the collateral history, and a fitness opinion given without completing the neuropsychiatric workup is not defensible. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Diagnose kleptomania and start naltrexone with psychological follow-up arranged
options.rationale: Kleptomania requires a build-up of tension before the theft and pleasure or relief at the time, both of which she explicitly denies, and it usually begins in adolescence or early adult life rather than in the seventh decade with new behavioural change. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Diagnose a depressive episode and start an antidepressant with review in 6 weeks
options.rationale: Apathy and social withdrawal in frontotemporal dementia are frequently misread as depression, but neither she nor her husband reports low mood, and the disinhibition, dietary change and loss of empathy do not fit a depressive episode. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

options.text: Arrange neuropsychological assessment with magnetic resonance imaging of the brain
options.rationale: New criminal behaviour committed openly without concealment, together with loss of empathy, dietary change towards sweet foods, and executive deficits on a preserved overall cognitive score, is the recognisable behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia picture, and neuropsychological testing with structural imaging is the appropriate workup. Bedside screening tools are insensitive to this syndrome because memory and orientation are preserved early, so a near-normal score cannot be used to exclude it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia
Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia clinical information

options.text: Refer for cognitive behavioural therapy targeting impulse control and offending behaviour
options.rationale: Psychological treatment for impulse control presumes intact capacity to learn and apply strategies, which is undermined by the executive impairment demonstrated here, and it would proceed without a diagnosis. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia

explanation.summary: New antisocial or criminal behaviour beginning in mid to later life with no prior history is a neuropsychiatric red flag, and behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia is the diagnosis most often missed in this presentation. Its core features are early behavioural disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, perseverative or ritualistic behaviour, hyperorality with a shift towards sweet foods, and executive dysfunction with relative preservation of memory and visuospatial function. That preservation is exactly why brief bedside screening tools perform poorly and why formal neuropsychological assessment is needed. Structural imaging typically shows frontal and anterior temporal atrophy, and functional imaging can help where structural imaging is equivocal. Recognition matters legally as well as clinically, because it bears on fitness to plead, on criminal responsibility and on decisions about guardianship and driving, and it redirects the family from blame towards support and planning.
key_points: New offending in mid to later life without prior history should prompt a neuropsychiatric assessment
Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia features disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy and a shift towards sweet foods
Memory and orientation are preserved early, so bedside screening scores are often near normal
Formal neuropsychological testing plus structural imaging is the appropriate workup
Diagnosis has direct forensic implications for fitness to plead and criminal responsibility
explanation.pearls: Offences in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia are characteristically committed in the open with no attempt at concealment and no apparent concern about consequences, which is the behavioural signature that most reliably separates them from ordinary offending.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources for frontotemporal dementia
Dementia Australia: Frontotemporal dementia clinical information

subtopic_detail: Legal pathway for urgent surgery refused by an objecting patient already on a community treatment order
stem:
You are the consultation liaison psychiatry registrar at a New South Wales hospital. The vascular surgical team asks you to see a 58-year-old woman with chronic schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes who has been admitted with a black, foul-smelling right forefoot.

The surgeons advise a below knee amputation within the next 48 hours. Without it they expect progression to systemic sepsis, though she is currently apyrexial and haemodynamically stable with a lactate of 1.2 mmol/L (below 2.0).

She has been on a community treatment order for 6 years and receives a fortnightly depot. She refuses the operation, telling you that the leg will heal itself because a voice on the radio told her the blackness is a sign of healing. She cannot repeat back that the surgeons believe she may die without surgery, and returns to the radio each time you explain it.

Her husband of 30 years is at the bedside, supports the surgery and says he will sign whatever is needed. She says clearly that she does not want an operation and does not want anyone else deciding for her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Black malodorous right forefoot with proximal demarcation, no cellulitis above the ankle
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 1.2 mmol/L (below 2.0), white cell count 9.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C-reactive protein 42 mg/L (less than 5)
data_table.Mental state: Delusional belief that the leg will heal, unable to retain or weigh the information given, actively objects to surgery and to substitute decision making

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Document a formal capacity assessment and apply to the guardianship tribunal for consent
options.rationale: Capacity is decision specific, so it must be assessed and documented for this operation rather than inferred from her psychiatric diagnosis or her treatment order. In New South Wales the person responsible may consent for someone who lacks capacity, but that authority falls away when the patient objects to the treatment, and consent must then be sought from the guardianship tribunal. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

options.text: Authorise the amputation under the Mental Health Act, since she is already an involuntary patient
options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for mental illness only, and a community treatment order confers no authority over surgical or other physical health treatment. This is the most tempting wrong branch because the legal framework is already in place for a different purpose. (Source: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.text: Obtain written consent from her husband as the person responsible and proceed to theatre
options.rationale: The husband would ordinarily be the person responsible and could consent for someone lacking capacity, but the legislation expressly removes that authority once the patient objects to the treatment, which she has done clearly and repeatedly. (Source: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.text: Proceed to theatre under the emergency provisions without seeking any further authorisation
options.rationale: Emergency provisions cover treatment needed urgently to save life or prevent serious damage when there is no time to obtain consent, and with a normal lactate, no fever and a 48-hour window there is time to follow the proper process. (Source: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual)
source_refs: NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual

options.text: Accept her refusal as an autonomous decision and document that she declined the surgery
options.rationale: Accepting a refusal requires the person to be able to understand, retain, weigh and communicate the decision, and she cannot retain or weigh the central fact that she may die, because a delusional belief displaces it. (Source: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent)
source_refs: RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

explanation.summary: This scenario turns on keeping three legal frameworks separate: mental health legislation, which authorises treatment for mental illness; guardianship legislation, which governs consent to medical treatment for adults who cannot consent for themselves; and the common law emergency doctrine. A community treatment order or involuntary status under mental health legislation gives no authority to treat a physical illness, a point frequently misunderstood on medical and surgical wards. Capacity is decision specific and time specific, and it is assessed against the ability to understand the information, retain it, weigh it in the balance and communicate a choice, not against whether the clinician agrees with the outcome. In New South Wales the person responsible hierarchy allows a spouse, carer or relative to consent for major medical treatment, but that pathway closes when the patient objects, at which point the guardianship tribunal must decide. A psychotic illness does not by itself remove capacity, but it does so where the delusional content directly displaces the relevant reasoning, as it does here.
key_points: Mental health legislation authorises treatment for mental illness only, never for physical illness
Capacity is decision specific and rests on understanding, retaining, weighing and communicating
The person responsible can consent for major medical treatment, but not when the patient objects
An objecting patient without capacity requires an application to the guardianship tribunal
A psychiatric diagnosis never removes capacity by itself; the delusional content must displace the relevant reasoning
explanation.pearls: Terminology and thresholds differ by jurisdiction: New South Wales uses the person responsible under the Guardianship Act, Victoria uses a medical treatment decision maker under its own legislation, so state the state before naming the substitute decision maker.

sources.label: NSW Guardianship Act 1987 and NSW Health consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
NSW Health: Consent to medical and healthcare treatment manual
RANZCP: Clinical practice resources on capacity and consent

subtopic_detail: Venesection target in a newly diagnosed C282Y homozygote with iron overload
stem:
A 48-year-old man attends your general practice to discuss abnormal blood results. He came in 2 months ago complaining of tiredness and aching in his right hip and in the knuckles at the base of his index and middle fingers on both hands.

He drinks four standard drinks a week, has never injected drugs and takes no supplements or over-the-counter preparations. He has no past history of blood transfusion. His father died at 62 of liver disease that was never fully explained.

His ferritin is 1180 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 68 per cent (15-45), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4) and full blood count within normal limits. HFE genotyping reports C282Y homozygosity. Transient elastography gives a liver stiffness of 5.2 kPa, which the report describes as normal.

data_table.Examination: Tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally, no hepatomegaly, no skin pigmentation change
data_table.Investigations: Ferritin 1180 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 68% (15-45), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), C-reactive protein 3 mg/L (less than 5), fasting glucose 5.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), full blood count within normal limits, HFE C282Y homozygous
data_table.Imaging: Transient elastography liver stiffness 5.2 kPa, reported as normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Dietary iron restriction with avoidance of red meat, and repeat ferritin in 6 months
options.rationale: Dietary measures shift iron balance only marginally and cannot clear a body iron burden of this size; avoiding uncooked shellfish and iron supplements is sensible advice but is not treatment. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

options.text: Deferasirox orally with monthly monitoring of renal function and ferritin response
options.rationale: Oral iron chelation is used where venesection is impossible, most often in transfusion dependent anaemias, and it is far more expensive and more toxic than removing blood from a man with normal haemoglobin. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Weekly venesection until the ferritin falls to between 50 and 100 micrograms per litre
options.rationale: Venesection is first line for hereditary haemochromatosis with iron overload, removing about 250 mg of iron per 500 mL unit, and the induction target is a ferritin of 50 to 100 micrograms per litre before moving to maintenance every 3 to 4 months. Treatment begins on the ferritin and saturation results without waiting for liver biopsy, which no longer has a routine diagnostic role. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update
Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal

options.text: Desferrioxamine by subcutaneous infusion five nights a week with ferritin monitoring
options.rationale: Parenteral chelation imposes a nightly infusion burden and ocular and auditory toxicity for a problem that venesection solves simply, and it is reserved for iron overload with anaemia or cardiac decompensation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Venesection only if a liver biopsy demonstrates established fibrosis on histological staging
options.rationale: Gating treatment on biopsy delays therapy in a man who already has symptoms and a ferritin above 1000 micrograms per litre, and biopsy is now reserved for cases where the diagnosis or the fibrosis stage is genuinely uncertain. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update)
source_refs: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

explanation.summary: Hereditary haemochromatosis is the commonest inherited disorder in Australians of northern European ancestry, with about 1 in 200 homozygous for the C282Y variant, although clinical penetrance is well under half. A raised transferrin saturation is the earliest biochemical abnormality and is more specific than ferritin, which rises in inflammation, alcohol excess and fatty liver, so both are needed to interpret suspected iron overload. The classic second and third metacarpophalangeal arthropathy is one of the few reasonably specific clinical signs and, unlike liver and endocrine damage, it does not reliably improve with venesection. A ferritin above 1000 micrograms per litre is the threshold that predicts significant fibrosis and triggers assessment of the liver, now usually with elastography rather than biopsy. First-degree relatives should be offered HFE genotyping and iron studies, since early treatment prevents cirrhosis, diabetes and cardiomyopathy entirely.
key_points: Transferrin saturation is the earliest and most specific marker; ferritin alone is confounded by inflammation and alcohol
Induction venesection is weekly until ferritin reaches 50 to 100 micrograms per litre, then maintenance every 3 to 4 months
Each 500 mL unit removes approximately 250 mg of iron
A ferritin above 1000 micrograms per litre predicts significant fibrosis and prompts liver assessment, now usually by elastography
Screen first-degree relatives with HFE genotyping and iron studies
explanation.pearls: Once cirrhosis is established, haemochromatosis patients need 6-monthly hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance for life, because venesection lowers but does not abolish that risk even after the ferritin normalises.

sources.label: Gastroenterological Society of Australia: Haemochromatosis clinical update

subtopic_detail: Treatment of recurrent facial swelling without urticaria unresponsive to adrenaline
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 29-year-old woman presents with swelling of her lower lip and tongue that has developed gradually over the past 6 hours.

This is her third such episode in 2 years. On the previous two occasions she was treated as anaphylaxis and received intramuscular adrenaline, intravenous hydrocortisone and an antihistamine, with no change in the swelling, which resolved over about 3 days each time. She reports no itch and there is no rash anywhere on her body.

She has eaten nothing unusual, has started no new medication and takes no angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor. Her mother has had similar episodes since her twenties and had an emergency laparotomy at 30 for abdominal pain that found nothing.

On examination her tongue and lower lip are swollen, her voice is normal, there is no stridor and she is protecting her own airway. Her C4 level from the last admission was recorded as 0.06 g/L (0.15-0.53). The anaesthetic registrar is aware and the resuscitation bay is prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Non-pitting swelling of the lower lip and tongue, no urticaria anywhere, no stridor, normal phonation
data_table.Investigations: C4 0.06 g/L (0.15-0.53) recorded at the previous admission

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Adrenaline 500 micrograms intramuscularly, repeated at 5-minute intervals as needed
options.rationale: Adrenaline is the correct treatment for mast cell mediated angioedema, but bradykinin mediated swelling does not respond to it, as her two previous admissions demonstrated. It is still given while the diagnosis is uncertain, since failing to treat true anaphylaxis is the more dangerous error. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

options.text: Hydrocortisone 200 mg intravenously with promethazine 25 mg given intravenously
options.rationale: Corticosteroids and antihistamines act on histamine driven pathways and have no effect on bradykinin mediated angioedema, which is why the previous admissions produced no response. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 2 units intravenously with close observation of the airway
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma contains C1 esterase inhibitor and is a recognised last resort where specific therapy is unavailable, but it also supplies substrate that can occasionally worsen the attack, so it is not the treatment of choice in a hospital with access to concentrate. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

options.text: C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate intravenously with close observation of the airway
options.rationale: A low C4 with recurrent non-itchy, non-urticarial angioedema unresponsive to adrenaline and steroids, in a family with the same pattern, indicates hereditary angioedema, in which plasma-derived C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate replaces the deficient protein and terminates the attack. Any laryngeal or tongue involvement is treated as an emergency because airway attacks can progress over hours. (Source: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper)
source_refs: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper
Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mg with intravenous dexamethasone and continuous observation
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema of inflammatory or allergic origin and buys time in croup or anaphylaxis, but it does not reverse a bradykinin mediated process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory

explanation.summary: Angioedema divides into histamine mediated forms, which itch, often come with urticaria and respond to adrenaline, antihistamines and corticosteroids, and bradykinin mediated forms, which do not itch, have no urticaria, evolve over hours and respond to none of those drugs. Hereditary angioedema results from deficiency or dysfunction of C1 esterase inhibitor and is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, so a family history of unexplained swelling or of a negative laparotomy for recurrent abdominal pain is highly suggestive. Screening is with a C4 level, which is low both during and between attacks, followed by C1 inhibitor antigenic and functional assays. Acute attacks involving the airway are treated with C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant, a bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist, and every patient should carry on-demand therapy. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor associated angioedema shares the bradykinin mechanism and the failure to respond to adrenaline, which is why that drug history is always sought.
key_points: No itch, no urticaria and no response to adrenaline points to a bradykinin mediated mechanism
A low C4 is the screening test, low both during and between attacks
C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate or icatibant terminates an acute attack; steroids and antihistamines do not
Autosomal dominant inheritance means a family history of swelling or negative laparotomy is common
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors cause an acquired bradykinin mediated angioedema with the same non-response
explanation.pearls: Laryngeal attacks carry a historical mortality of around 30 per cent in untreated hereditary angioedema, so any tongue or throat involvement is treated immediately with specific therapy and observed in a setting capable of securing a surgical airway.

sources.label: Australasian Society of Clinical Immunology and Allergy: Hereditary angioedema position paper

subtopic_detail: Management of a pulmonary exacerbation in an adult with chronic Pseudomonas colonisation
stem:
You are the respiratory registrar in a tertiary adult clinic. A 27-year-old woman with cystic fibrosis attends as a walk-in, having felt progressively worse over 10 days.

She reports that her sputum has doubled in volume and turned dark green, and that she is coughing through the night and has lost 3 kg. She has no fever and no pleuritic pain. She takes a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulator, pancreatic enzyme replacement and inhaled hypertonic saline.

Her best forced expiratory volume in 1 second over the past year was 62 per cent predicted; today it is 48 per cent predicted. Her sputum has repeatedly grown mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa over the past 3 years, with sensitivities showing susceptibility to ceftazidime and tobramycin and resistance to ciprofloxacin. Her chest radiograph shows her usual upper lobe bronchiectatic changes without a new consolidation or pneumothorax. Her oxygen saturation is 94 per cent on room air.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 98/min, blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Spirometry: Forced expiratory volume in 1 second 48% predicted today, against a best of 62% predicted in the past year
data_table.Microbiology: Repeated mucoid Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptible to ceftazidime and tobramycin, resistant to ciprofloxacin
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph shows established upper lobe bronchiectasis with no new consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin with clavulanate for 14 days at home with clinic review afterwards
options.rationale: Amoxicillin with clavulanate has no useful activity against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and would not cover the organism repeatedly isolated from her sputum. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral prednisolone 30 mg daily for 7 days with intensified airway clearance at home
options.rationale: Systemic corticosteroids are used in cystic fibrosis for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, not for a routine bacterial exacerbation, and they do not treat the infection driving her decline. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 750 mg twice daily for 14 days at home with clinic review afterwards
options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin is the usual home option for a mild Pseudomonas exacerbation, but her isolate is reported resistant and a 14-point fall in forced expiratory volume with weight loss is beyond what home oral therapy manages. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care

options.text: Nebulised tobramycin alone for a 28-day cycle with clinic review at the end of the course
options.rationale: Inhaled tobramycin is maintenance suppressive therapy for chronic colonisation rather than treatment of an acute exacerbation, and relying on it alone leaves a significant lung function decline untreated. The distinction is between suppression between exacerbations and eradication of an acute flare. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care

options.text: Admit for intravenous ceftazidime with tobramycin and intensified airway clearance
options.rationale: A fall of more than 10 per cent in forced expiratory volume with increased sputum volume and purulence and weight loss defines a significant pulmonary exacerbation, treated with two intravenous antipseudomonal agents from different classes for 14 days alongside intensified physiotherapy and nutritional support. Dual therapy is used to limit emergence of resistance during treatment of a chronically colonised airway. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care
Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Pulmonary exacerbations drive the long-term decline in cystic fibrosis, and each one that is not fully treated tends to leave the patient with a lower baseline lung function than before. The diagnosis is clinical, resting on increased cough and sputum volume or purulence, breathlessness, weight loss and a fall in forced expiratory volume in 1 second, with a drop of more than 10 per cent from baseline being a widely used threshold for intravenous therapy. Antibiotic choice is driven by the individual patient's sputum culture history rather than by empirical protocols, since airway flora become highly individualised over years. Two antipseudomonal agents from different classes are used to reduce emergent resistance, typically a beta-lactam with an aminoglycoside, and aminoglycoside levels require monitoring given cumulative nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity across a lifetime of courses. Airway clearance, nutrition and review of modulator therapy are treated as equal parts of the admission rather than as extras.
key_points: A fall of more than 10 per cent in forced expiratory volume with increased sputum signals a significant exacerbation
Treat with two intravenous antipseudomonal agents from different classes, usually for 14 days
Select antibiotics from the patient's own sputum culture and sensitivity history
Inhaled tobramycin is chronic suppression, not treatment of an acute exacerbation
Intensify airway clearance and address nutrition as part of the same admission
explanation.pearls: Isolation of Burkholderia cepacia complex changes everything: it is associated with accelerated decline and, for some genomovars, exclusion from lung transplantation, which is why strict segregation between cystic fibrosis patients is enforced in Australian clinics.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Cystic fibrosis standards of care
